claims.text: Coupling high-accuracy ab initio calculations with CALPHAD can accurately predict melting temperatures across the high-entropy-alloy family.
The integrated approach can accurately predict fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
The target materials are high-entropy or multi-principal-element alloys in a solid-solution state near melting.
Configurational entropy dominates in these solid-solution alloys near their melting temperature.
Detailed DFT simulations can capture electronic, vibrational, and magnetic contributions near melting.
CALPHAD can use ab initio inputs to generate continuous phase diagrams and extrapolate liquid-phase properties.
Near melting, the entropy term dominates the Gibbs free energy and atomic disorder is maximized.
The method should be applied to compositionally complex alloys with minimal nanoprecipitate effects.
Configurational disorder and short-range order affect the energy landscape and entropy contributions to Gibbs free energy.
DFT provides accurate energy landscapes, phonon contributions, electronic structure, one-electron entropy, and finite-temperature effects.
CALPHAD interpolates atomistic data into full thermodynamic descriptions that predict changes in melting temperature, enthalpy, entropy, and volume.
Predicted fusion properties will agree with DSC and density measurements within approximately ±10–15% across a range of high-entropy alloys.
Experimental DSC data are available as a baseline for reference Cantor-alloy and nickel systems.
Previously validated computational studies on Cantor alloys and Ni-based superalloys provide a performance baseline.
The approach is applicable to high-entropy alloys exhibiting predominantly random solid-solution behavior at high temperature.
Strong local ordering or nanoprecipitation before melting may cause significant prediction errors.
Uncertainty remains in the treatment of liquid dynamics and short-range ordering just below melting.
Consistent deviations greater than ±20% between measured and predicted thermodynamic properties would falsify the proposed approach.
